the case for all n ≥ m . Put m = max({m1 , m′1 , ..., mi , m′i , m′′ }), then we get an element in
                     ′′     ′′            ′′′

hT r(Gbm′′′ )i that is an involution, and this is a contradiction to the fact that the pair (G                     bm′′′ )
                                                                                                           bm′′′ , X
is in class ST ′0 (p).                                                                                                 

   Hence, the group Ḡ is almost sharply 2-transitive of characteristic p. Moreover, by construction,
Ḡ has no translation of inﬁnite order, and thus it belongs to the class ST (p). This ﬁnishes the
proof of Proposition 2.15.
   We end this section with the following result, which implies (by Theorem 2.11) that the groups
constructed in Theorem 2.17 do not split.

Lemma 5.17. Ḡ contains non-commuting translations.

Proof. Consequence (4) of Theorem 4.28 implies in particular that N̄ is inﬁnite. Since this subgroup
is generated by translations of Ḡ, and in this group the centralizer of every translation is cyclic of
order p (by Condition (4) of the deﬁnition of class ST (p)) then N̄ must have a pair of translations
that do not commute.                                                                                 
32                           MARCO AMELIO, SIMON ANDRÉ & KATRIN TENT


                                    6. Proof of Proposition 2.14
     In this section we prove Proposition 2.14, which we recall for convenience.
Proposition 2.14. Let p be an odd prime number and let G be a group in ST (p).
   (1) Let (r, s), (r′ , s′ ) ∈ I(G)(2) with (r, s) of p-affine type, and (r′ , s′ ) of p-minimal type and
                                   G∗ = hG, t | trt−1 = r′ , tst−1 = s′ i.
    (2) Let H be a non-trivial group without 2-torsion and G∗ = G ∗ H.
Let X denote the corresponding Bass-Serre tree. Then (G∗ , X) belongs to ST ′ (p).
     We ﬁrst observe the following general result.
Lemma 6.1. Let G be a group and let (K, K ′ ) be a quasi-malnormal pair (see Definition 2.6)
of isomorphic subgroups of G. Let α : K → K ′ be an isomorphism, and consider the group
G∗ = hG, t | tkt−1 = α(k)i. Let X be the corresponding Bass-Serre tree. Then stabilizers of paths
with at least three edges in X have order at most two.
Proof. Let v denote the vertex of X ﬁxed by G. Let [v1 , v2 , v3 , v4 ] be a path of length 3 in the tree
X (with d(vi , vi+1 ) = 1). We will prove that the (global) stabilizer of this path has order at most 2.
Since G∗ acts transitively on the (non-oriented) edges of X, we can assume that [v2 , v3 ] = [v, t−1 v]
or [v2 , v3 ] = [t−1 v, v]. Without loss of generality, suppose that [v2 , v3 ] = [v, t−1 v]. The stabilizer of
this edge is G ∩ t−1 Gt = K. Since the vertices v1 and v2 = v are adjacent, there exists an element
g ∈ G such that v1 = gt−1 v or v1 = gtv, thus the stabilizer of the path [v1 , v2 , v3 ] is gKg −1 ∩ K or
gK ′ g −1 ∩ K, hence it has order at most 2 since the pair (K, K ′ ) is quasi-malnormal.                     
Proof of Proposition 2.14. We treat both cases uniformly, so let G ∈ ST (p), and let G∗ denote
either the HNN extension or the free product deﬁned in Proposition 2.14, let X denote the corre-
sponding Bass-Serre tree and deﬁne Q = T r(G∗ ) and N = hT r(G)i. We need to show that G is
almost sharply 2-transitive of characteristic p and satisﬁes the conditions given in Deﬁnition 2.13
for ST ′ (p).
  To see that G∗ is almost sharply 2-transitive of characteristic p, we ﬁrst verify Condition (4’) of
Deﬁnition 2.13 of ST ′ (p) as this condition will be used in the proof of almost sharply 2-transitivity.
(4’): no loxodromic element of G∗ normalizes a non-trivial ﬁnite subgroup of order > 2.
   Let F be a ﬁnite subgroup of G∗ of order > 2. We will prove that NG∗ (F ) is elliptic in the
Bass-Serre tree X. First, note that the ﬁxed-point set Y ⊂ X of F is preserved by NG∗ (F ).
   If G∗ = G ∗ H, then Y is a point, and thus NG∗ (F ) ﬁxes this point as well.
   If G∗ is the HNN extension deﬁned in Proposition 2.14 then, by Lemmas 2.7 and 6.1, the subtree
Y has diameter at most two. If Y is a point, then NG∗ (F ) ﬁxes this point. If Y has diameter one,
then it consists of two vertices joined by an edge e, and NG∗ (F ) ﬁxes the edge e as well. If Y has
diameter two, then NG∗ (F ) ﬁxes the midpoint of this subtree.
     We now show that G∗ is almost sharply 2-transitive as deﬁned in Deﬁnition 2.4.
(1): every translation is either of order p or of inﬁnite order, and every pair (r, s) ∈ I(G∗ )(2) such
that rs has order p is either of p-aﬃne type or of p-minimal type.
   Let g = rs be a translation, where r, s denote two distinct involutions of G∗ . If r and s have
a common ﬁxed in the tree X, then their product g is contained in a conjugate of G, and thus it
has order p and it is either of p-aﬃne type or of p-minimal type since G belongs to ST (p) (and
by Condition (4’) above, the normalizer of the subgroup it generates is elliptic). If r and s do not
have a common ﬁxed point, then g is loxodromic (and thus it has inﬁnite order).
(2): the subgroup N ∗ = hT r(G∗ )i contains no involution.
  First, suppose that G∗ = G ∗ H, where H has no involution, as in Proposition 2.14. Assume
towards a contradiction that there is an involution in N ∗ , or equivalently, an odd number of
           NON-SPLIT SHARPLY 2-TRANSITIVE GROUPS OF ODD POSITIVE CHARACTERISTIC                             33


involutions r1 , . . . , rk of G∗ such that r1 · · · rk = 1. Since H has no involution, every ri is conjugate
to an involution of G. Let π ⋆ : G∗ ։ G denote the map obtained by killing the free factor H. Then
π ⋆ (r1 · · · rk ) = 1, and π ⋆ (r1 · · · rk ) is a product of an odd number of involutions in G, contradicting
the assumption that N has no involution (since G belongs to ST (p)).
    Then, suppose that G∗ is the HNN extension deﬁned in Proposition 2.14. The argument is the
same as in the previous case, but a bit more involved. Assume towards a contradiction that there
is an involution in N ∗ , or equivalently, an odd number of involutions r1 , . . . , rk of G∗ such that
r1 · · · rk = 1. Consider the quotient of G∗ by the normal subgroup generated by the stable letter
                                                                        ∗
t of the HNN extension, that is, the group G′ = G∗ /htiG , and call π ⋆ : G∗ ։ G′ the quotient
                          ′
map. Notice that G can also be obtained as the quotient of G by the relations k = α(k), that is
G′ ∼ = G/hk −1 α(k) : k ∈ KiG . We will identify these isomorphic groups, and call π : G ։ G′ the
quotient map. Note that the kernel of π is contained in N = hT r(G)i. By assumption G belongs
to ST (p), thus N contains no involution. Hence no involution of G is mapped to the identity by π.
Furthermore, the restriction of π ⋆ to G coincides with π, and every involution of G∗ is conjugate
to an involution of G. Therefore, no involution of G∗ is mapped to the identity by π ⋆ . Thus, the
image π ⋆ (r1 ...rk ) is a (trivial) product of an odd number of involutions of G′ . Moreover, every
preimage of π ⋆ (r1 ...rk ) in G will be a product of an odd number of involutions. That is, there is
an involution in N = hT r(G)i, and we arrive at a contradiction.
(3): the set of pairs (r, s) ∈ I(G∗ )(2) of p-aﬃne type is non-empty and G∗ acts transitively on it.
   First, note that this set is non-empty since G is contained in G∗ . Then, if (r, s) ∈ I(G∗ )(2) is of
p-aﬃne type then hr, si is ﬁnite, thus it is elliptic in the tree X. It follows that hr, si is contained
in a conjugate of G, and the conclusion follows from the fact that G belongs to ST (p).
(4): for (r, s) ∈ I(G∗ )(2) , Cen(rs) is cyclic and generated by a translation.
   If rs is elliptic then its centralizer is elliptic in the tree X by Condition (4’) above, and the
conclusion follows from the fact that G belongs to ST (p).
   If rs is loxodromic then it is contained in a (unique) maximal loxodromic subgroup of G∗ ,
which is isomorphic to D∞ (indeed, exactly as in Remark 5.9, since G∗ satisﬁes Condition (1)
and Condition (4’), every loxodromic subgroup of G∗ is isomorphic to Z or C2 × Z or D∞ or
C4 ∗C2 C4 , and D∞ is the only group in this list that contains two distinct involutions), and thus
the centralizer of rs is cyclic inﬁnite, generated by a translation.
   It is left to verify Conditions (1’)–(3’) of Deﬁnition 2.13 of ST ′ (p).
(1’): the action of G∗ on X is acylindrical (and non-elementary).
   If G∗ is the HNN extension deﬁned in Proposition 2.14, then by Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 6.1
stabilizers of paths with at least three edges in X have order at most two. If G∗ = G∗H, stabilizers
of edges are trivial. In both cases, one easily sees that the action of G∗ on X is acylindrical, and
the fact that the action is non-elementary is clear.
(2’): e(N, X) = 1, rinj (Q, X) ≥ 1, ν(N, X) ≤ 5 and A(N, X) = 0.
   Note that since the space X is 0-hyperbolic, it follows from Lemma 3.22 that [g]∞ = [g] for all
g ∈ G∗ , and thus rinj (Q, X) = inf({[g] : g ∈ Q, g loxodromic}). Hence, since X is a simplicial tree,
we immediately get rinj (Q, X) ≥ 1 (in fact, it can be proved that rinj (Q, X) = 2).
   Then, let us prove that ν(N, X) ≤ 5. The parameters of the deﬁnition of an acylindrical action
(see Deﬁnition 3.28) corresponding to ε = 97δ can be taken to be L = 3 and M = 2 in the case
where G∗ is the HNN extension deﬁned in Proposition 2.14 (since stabilizers of paths with at least
three edges in X have order at most two), and L = M = 1 in the case where G∗ = G ∗ H. In both
cases, the bound ν(N, X) ≤ 5 follows readily from Lemma 4.5.
   To see that e(N, X) = 1, by Remark 4.3 it is suﬃcient to prove that every loxodromic subgroup
E of N is cyclic. As in the proof of Condition (4), we have that E is isomorphic to one of the
34                             MARCO AMELIO, SIMON ANDRÉ & KATRIN TENT


following four groups: Z, C2 × Z, D∞ or C4 ∗C2 C4 . But N ∗ has no involution (by Condition (2)),
and thus E is necessarily isomorphic to Z.
   Last, let us prove that A(N, X) = 0. First notice that, since our space X is 0-hyperbolic, the
axis of an element g is the set Ag = {x ∈ X : d(x, g · x) = [g]}. Also, since ν = ν(N, X) is ﬁnite,
we are looking at tuples (g0 , . . . , gν ) of elements with [gi ] = 0 for all i ∈ {0, . . . , ν} (that is, tuples
of elliptic elements) such that they do not generate an elementary subgroup. In this case, Agi is
just the ﬁxed-point set of gi , and A(g0 , . . . , gν ) = diam(Ag0 ∩ · · · ∩ Agν ) is the diameter of the
intersection of their ﬁxed-point sets. If all these elliptic elements have a ﬁxed point in common,
then every element of hg0 , . . . , gν i will also ﬁx this point, and therefore, they would generate an
elementary subgroup. That is, we only need to consider tuples (g0 , . . . , gν ) of elliptic elements such
that Ag0 ∩ · · · ∩ Agν = ∅. Thus, A(g0 , . . . , gν ) = 0, and therefore, A(N, X) = 0.
(3’): translations of inﬁnite order of G∗ are loxodromic for their action on X.
   Let g = rs be a translation, where r, s denote two distinct involutions of G∗ . If r and s have a
common ﬁxed point v ∈ X, then their product g ﬁxes v as well. Hence g is contained in a conjugate
of G (namely the stabilizer of v in G∗ ), and thus it has order p since G belongs to ST (p). If r and
s do not have a common ﬁxed point, then g is loxodromic (and thus it has inﬁnite order).
     This ﬁnishes the proof of Proposition 2.14 and thus of Theorem 1.1.                                       

                                 Appendix A. Proof of Lemma 3.10
   In this appendix we include the proof of Lemma 3.10. For the sake of completeness, we will also
restate this result.
Lemma A.1. Let X be a δ-hyperbolic metric space, x, y ∈ X. Let γ be a (1, ℓ)-quasi-geodesic
connecting x to y for ℓ ≥ 0. Let p ∈ X be a point such that
(1)                                 d(x, p) + d(p, y) ≤ d(x, y) + 2δ + 3ℓ.
Then, d(p, γ) ≤ 4δ + 8ℓ.
Proof. Without loss of generality, we can assume that d(x, p) ≤ d(y, p). If we have d(x, p) ≥ d(x, y),
then we get that d(y, p) ≤ 2δ + 3ℓ and we are done. Similarly, if we assume d(y, p) ≥ d(x, y), then
we get that d(x, p) ≤ 2δ + 3ℓ.
   Now, assume that
                                 max({d(x, p), d(y, p)}) < d(x, y).
Take a point z ∈ γ such that
(2)                                    d(p, y) ≤ d(z, y) ≤ d(p, y) + ℓ.
Since X is δ-hyperbolic, we have that
(3)                                 hx, yip ≥ min{hx, zip , hy, zip } − δ.
Combining Deﬁnition 3.7 with the second inequality of (2) we get
                         1                                          1                     ℓ
(4)      hx, zip − hy, zip =
                           (d(x, p) − d(x, z) − d(y, p) + d(y, z)) ≤ (d(x, p) − d(x, z)) + .
                         2                                          2                     2
Now, inequality (1) and the second inequality of (2) give
(5)                    d(x, p) − 2δ − 3l ≤ d(x, y) − d(y, p) ≤ d(x, y) − d(y, z) + ℓ,
and this together with the triangle inequality imply
(6)                                    d(x, p) − 2δ − 3ℓ ≤ d(x, z) + ℓ.
Therefore, inequalities (4) and (6) yield
                                                                 5
(7)                                       hx, zip − hy, zip ≤ δ + ℓ.
                                                                 2
                                             REFERENCES                                      35


From inequalities (3) and (7) we get
                                                      5
(8)                                hx, yip ≥ hx, zip − ℓ − 2δ.
                                                      2
Inequality (8) together with Deﬁnition 3.7 yield
                           d(y, p) − d(x, y) ≥ d(z, p) − d(x, z) − 5ℓ − 4δ,
and thus
(9)                        d(y, p) − d(x, y) + d(x, z) ≥ d(z, p) − 5ℓ − 4δ.
Also, since z ∈ γ we have that
                                   d(x, z) + d(z, y) ≤ d(x, y) + 3ℓ,
and in consequence,
(10)                              d(x, z) − d(x, y) ≤ −d(z, y) + 3ℓ.
Therefore, combining inequalities (9) and (10) we obtain
(11)                             d(y, p) − d(z, y) ≥ d(z, p) − 8ℓ − 4δ.
The ﬁrst inequality of (2) and inequalitiy (11) imply that d(z, p) ≤ 8ℓ + 4δ.                
